nameStory: This delicate autumn crocus is named after Theodor Kotschy, a 19th-century Austrian botanist who explored the mountains of Turkey and the Middle East. Kotschy was known for his daring plant-collecting expeditions in remote regions, and this pale purple beauty was among his discoveries in the rugged landscapes of Asia Minor.
description: Kotschy's Crocus is a small, autumn-blooming bulb that reaches only about 4 inches tall. Unlike most crocuses that herald spring, this little charmer produces its pale lilac-blue flowers in fall, creating unexpected splashes of color in the autumn garden. The flowers appear first, followed by narrow, sword-like leaves that persist through winter and into the following spring.

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Pale lilac-blue, goblet-shaped flowers with six petals that feel papery and delicate to the touch, appearing in autumn rather than spring

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Narrow, sword-like leaves with a distinctive white stripe down the center, emerging after the flowers fade and persisting through winter

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Very low-growing bulb plant reaching only 3-4 inches tall, forming small clumps over time

idTips.label: Blooming Season
idTips.description: Flowers appear in fall (September-October), making it unusual among crocuses which typically bloom in spring

habitat: In New England, this is extremely rare as a garden escape or naturalized plant, found only in cultivated settings or areas where bulbs have been planted and persisted. It prefers well-drained soil and sunny to partially shaded locations, similar to other crocus species.

seasonality.spring: Sword-like leaves are visible and may still be green from the previous fall's growth before dying back in late spring.
seasonality.summer: Plant is completely dormant with no visible above-ground parts, resting as an underground bulb.
seasonality.fall: Pale lilac-blue flowers emerge directly from the ground in September-October, followed by new leaves appearing after blooming.
seasonality.winter: Fresh green leaves with white central stripes persist through winter, making this one of the few crocuses with winter foliage.

funFact: This backwards bloomer completely flips the script on spring bulbs by flowering in autumn and then growing its leaves through winter, essentially living its life in reverse compared to daffodils and tulips!
confusionNotes: Most easily confused with other autumn crocuses, but Kotschy's Crocus has distinctly pale lilac-blue flowers (not deep purple like Bieberstein's Crocus) and appears much later in fall than most spring-blooming escapees.
contextualKnowledge: With only one observation recorded in New England, this species is incredibly rare in our region and likely represents a single garden planting that has persisted or briefly naturalized rather than an established population.
compareHints: Unlike the common Spring Crocus which blooms in March-April with white, purple, or yellow flowers, Kotschy's Crocus blooms in fall with pale lilac-blue flowers. It's also much rarer than Woodland Crocus, which blooms earlier in spring and has more pointed petals with darker purple stripes.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Woodland crocus blooms earlier than the larger spring crocus (Crocus vernus) and has more delicate, slender flowers.
Spring crocus is larger than its cousin the snow crocus, which blooms slightly earlier and has smaller, more delicate flowers.
Spring crocus blooms slightly later than snow crocus and has more elongated, pointed petals compared to the broader, rounder petals of Dutch crocus.
Snow crocus is the smallest and earliest blooming of the common crocuses in New England.
Among New England crocuses, silvery crocus is distinguished by its particularly pale coloring and the dark striping on outer petals.
**Comparison details uncertain due to limited data.
Unlike the common spring crocuses found throughout New England, Bieberstein's crocus blooms in fall rather than spring.
Among New England crocuses, Sieber's crocus is distinguished by its orange gradient effect on the petals, which fades from the brilliant orange stamens down through the bottom third of each petal.
